questions.prompt: An active intrusion is happening right now. How should it be reported?
options: Immediate escalation
A routine report for next week
A council item for next month
Not at all, it may stop

questions.prompt: A false alarm that was already resolved last week. How should it be reported?
options: Immediate escalation at 2 AM
A routine report
An emergency council meeting
A call to every crew member

questions.prompt: A pattern of the same minor issue keeps recurring and may need a policy change. Where should it go?
options: Nowhere, it is minor
Straight to the MSSP
To the council
Wake the lead now

questions.prompt: Why not make every alert feel urgent?
options: Alerts can only be sent once
People learn to ignore alerts
The council forbids it outright
Urgent alerts cost more money

questions.prompt: What is the goal of a reporting structure?
options: The right event reaches the right person at the right speed
Every event wakes the security lead in the middle of the night
Only the most serious events are ever written down anywhere
Each crew member decides alone who should hear about it

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of change management?
options: Approve, request, verify, implement
Request, implement, approve, verify
Implement, verify, request, approve
Request, approve, implement, verify

questions.prompt: What happens in the verify step?
options: Someone signs off on the planned change
Someone proposes the change and the reason
The change is made on the live system
Confirm it worked and nothing else broke

questions.prompt: An unapproved change happened to work. Why is it still a risk?
options: Approved changes always run faster afterwards
Unapproved changes are deleted the next day
The change will certainly fail next time
Nobody with a wider view caught conflicts

questions.prompt: "An unapproved change that happens to work is…" what?
options: A new standard
A fine shortcut to keep
Luck, not process
Proof of real skill

questions.prompt: Who weighs the risk against the benefit before a change?
options: Someone with authority to approve
Any crew member who is nearby
The attacker who caused the issue
The person making the change alone

questions.prompt: What makes an acceptable use policy real?
options: Enforcement
A longer document
A new title
A signature only

questions.prompt: A first-time, minor, accidental breach of the AUP. What fits?
options: Ignoring it completely this time
A reminder and a note in the record
Disabling the account on the spot
Revoking every permission they have

questions.prompt: A deliberate breach for the third time this month, after two warnings. What fits?
options: Rewriting the AUP so the act is allowed
Nothing, since no real harm was done yet
A firmer response, like revoking access
Another gentle reminder, like the first two

questions.prompt: Why does consistent enforcement matter?
options: Consistency removes every risk
Consistency makes the logs much shorter
Policies only count if read aloud
Uneven enforcement erodes the policy

questions.prompt: What is an administrative control?
options: A firewall rule that blocks a port
A tool that enforces a rule on its own
A rule or review carried out by people
A password policy the system checks

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a technical control?
options: A firewall rule
A signed approval
An access review
A background check

questions.prompt: Which is an example of an administrative control?
options: An access-control list
A firewall rule on a port
A periodic access review
A rejected weak password

questions.prompt: Which question can a technical control NOT answer?
options: Is this port allowed through the firewall?
Should this person be trusted with it?
Does this file need a password to open it?
Is this password long enough to accept?

questions.prompt: Why does a security program need leadership's visible support?
options: Visible support replaces the need for a budget
Leaders are the only people who must follow the rules
Written endorsements are enough to run a program
Leaders who skip rules teach rules are optional

questions.prompt: What does resourcing a security program mean?
options: Giving it the time, budget and staff it needs
Buying the most expensive tool there is
Letting each department fund its own rules
Signing the policy and approving it with a nod

questions.prompt: A leader signs a policy, never funds it and bypasses it when it is inconvenient. What message does this send?
options: That the policy is ready for audit
That the policy does not really matter
That the policy is working very well indeed
That the crew should follow it more

questions.prompt: A leader refuses to skip the access log even when in a hurry. What is this?
options: Poor resourcing
Leading by example
A breach of the policy
Wasting time

questions.prompt: What does operational accountability mean?
options: Each department keeps its own budget
Each account is shared by a whole team of people
Each sensitive act traces to one person
Each change is approved by the council

questions.prompt: Three people share one shield-duty login. What does that break?
options: Accountability
Network bandwidth
Encryption
Availability

questions.prompt: Nothing bad has happened on a shared account yet. Why remove it anyway?
options: Shared accounts always slow the system down
Shared accounts cannot have strong passwords
The account will be hacked by tomorrow
You can't trace later what happened

questions.prompt: Removing a shared account assumes the crew is dishonest. Is that true?
options: No, it is about tracing, not distrust
No, it is about saving money on licences
Yes, it means that nobody is trusted
Yes, shared accounts mean that people lie

questions.prompt: What should replace a shared account?
options: A longer password on the same account
A guest account with no password
One named account for each person
A second shared account for backup

questions.prompt: Which control is enforced automatically and consistently?
options: An administrative control
A technical control
A verbal reminder
A council decision

questions.prompt: An implementer could not see a conflict with another system. Which step would have caught it?
options: Request
Verify
Implement
Approve

questions.prompt: Two people break the same rule; one is punished and one is ignored. What happens to the policy?
options: It becomes stronger
It loses its force
It is rewritten
It is unaffected
